transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Carlos Mendes (Redwood AE), Leah Park (Redwood SE), Jamal Khan (Acme Head of Platform), Priya Singh (Acme ML Eng), Evan Lee (Acme SRE), Marta Ruiz (Acme Product)

Summary:
Brief: POC scoping focused on latency and throughput SLO defintion for ACME Payments' fraud-detection reranking pipeline. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, benchmarking plan, required artifacts and timeline. Agreed to run a 1-week benchmark with Redwood-provided harness against customer traces.

Topics:
- Success criteria for POC (latency targets, throughput, cost envelope, quality thresholds)
- Workload sizing and representative traces (RPS, sequence length dist)
- Benchmarks: TTFT, TPOT, p95/p99 definitions & measurement windows
- Measurement plan: harness, metrics, sampling, cold vs warm cache, KV cache priming
- Timeline and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Carlos: okay everyone thanks for joining. quick intros — i'm carlos from Redwood, leah's our SE today.
[00:07] Jamal: jamal here, head of platform at acme, priya and evan are on from infra and ml, marta listening too.
[00:14] Leah: great, thanks. goal for today is to scope the poc around the latency/throughput SLOs you asked about and nail down what success looks like.
[00:21] Priya: yes, we want to validate that Redwood can meet our p95/p99 for our reranking step. currently we're using an internal tiny transformer but the latency is too high at peak, so we're evaluating moving to hosted inference or dedicated.
[00:35] Carlos: helpful. can you share current numbers? typical rps, request size, and latency tails?
[00:40] Priya: sure — our typical is 120 rps average, peaks at 350 rps for 10-15 minutes during batch settlement windows, sequence lengths for the reranker are usually 64-128 tokens, sometimes up to 256 on edge cases. p95 is around 210 ms, p99 around 430 ms — but that's for our current in-house instance; the generator upstream adds variable time.
[01:05] Evan: also we have a strict TTFT constraint for end-user flows: we need first-token under 150 ms ideally for interactive UI, but for back-office batch reranks TPOT is more important, so p95 for total completion should be under 600 ms.
[01:20] Carlos: ok good clarity. two things we often differentiate: TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time to produce output token / total-generation-time). For streaming interactive use TTFT is key; for batch rerank TPOT or end-to-end latency matters.
[01:36] Jamal: we probably need both measured. for the POC success we want two tracks: interactive endpoints (TTFT p95 < 150 ms, p99 < 300 ms) and batch endpoints (TPOT p95 < 600 ms, p99 < 900 ms) — are those realistic?
[01:52] Leah: depends on model variant and deployment mode. for a quantized 7B model on dedicated GPU we can typically hit those TTFT numbers with warm cache but p99 can be sensitive to cold-starts and queuing. we'll design the harness to measure cold vs warm and isolate queuing effects.
[02:10] Priya: what's your recommendation for the measurement windows? should we look at 5-minute windows or longer?
[02:15] Leah: recommend multiple windows: steady-state p95/p99 over 5-minute sliding windows during a sustained load, plus aggregate over the 1-week benchmark. Also capture TTFT distribution per request and measure prefix cache hit rate.
[02:30] Carlos: and we should capture queueing latency separately from inference time. Redwood's runtime exposes breakdowns: scheduling/queue wait, load time, kernel execution, and response serialization. we'll include those in the report.
[02:43] Jamal: good, we need that granularity for capacity planning. Another question: how do you suggest we size the benchmark? our daily average is 120 rps but we want to test 2x and 3x to plan for burst.
[02:56] Leah: typical POC plan: run steady-state tests at baseline (1x), 2x, and 3x of typical RPS for 10–15 minute sustained windows, then a stress test that ramps to peak for 30–60s to observe queueing and tail latency. we'll also run a cold cache run in the beginning and then a warm run.
[03:15] Priya: ok, and what about concurrency and batching? our upstream sends many small requests; batching could help but might increase TTFT.
[03:22] Carlos: right — there's a tradeoff. Redwood's optimizer suggests batching windows by latency SLO. For interactive endpoints we use small batch sizes or dynamic batching with tight latency limits to keep TTFT low. For batch endpoints we allow larger batch sizes and improve throughput (TPOT). We'll include recommended batching/quantization profiles in the POC deliverable.
[03:40] Jamal: we also care about model fallbacks in case capacity is constrained — e.g., fall back from 13B to 7B. will that change latency targets?
[03:46] Leah: yes, smaller models reduce kernel time; but quantization and pipeline also matter. For the POC we'll test at least two model variants representative of your production choices and measure both until we find the sweet spot for cost vs latency.
[04:00] Evan: network egress and VPC peering adds ~20-30 ms in our infra sometimes. can you run benchmarks from a private deployment or dedicated to reflect that?
[04:08] Carlos: yes we can run in Dedicated mode within your VPC (if you provision the peering) or we can simulate network latency in the harness; ideally you provide a test agent in your VPC and we run the client there so network effects are realistic.
[04:22] Priya: what about measurement definitions: for TTFT do we measure from request arrival at Redwood edge or from client's send time including network?
[04:28] Leah: we recommend measuring both. Primary POC SLOs should be client-observed latency (end-to-end) to reflect user experience. Secondary SLOs should be Redwood-edge observed breakdowns for diagnosis. We'll include both in the report and correlate them.
[04:43] Jamal: excellent. also we want p95 and p99 computed over non-overlapping 5-minute windows and then an aggregate for the workload — is that feasible?
[04:51] Leah: yes; we'll provide both sliding window and fixed window stats; we'll export raw histograms so you can compute quantiles yourself too.
[05:00] Carlos: let's talk success criteria: what must pass for you to consider the POC a success?
[05:05] Priya: success if for the interactive route TTFT p95 < 150ms and p99 < 300ms for at least 90% of steady-state windows at 1x and 2x load; and for batch route TPOT p95 < 600ms and p99 < 900ms at 1x load. secondarily, CPU/GPU utilization should be within cost envelope we defined — target is cost per 1M requests under $X (we'll share the number).
[05:29] Jamal: and quality — reranking accuracy shouldn't degrade more than 1% against our baseline. we'll add that as a quality criteria.
[05:36] Leah: noted. we'll include evaluation harness to run your prompt set and measure rerank metrics. please share the golden prompts and scoring criteria.
[05:45] Evan: what's your expected timeline to run the POC? we want results in 3 weeks ideally.
[05:50] Carlos: typical POC cycle: 1 week of setup (networking, traces, test agent), 1 week of benchmarking (runs at various loads), 1 week for analysis and recommendations. so 3 weeks is realistic assuming we get artifacts quickly.
[06:04] Priya: we can get traces and prompts within 3 business days.
[06:08] Carlos: perfect. on measurement plan specifics — we'll provide a harness that:
- accepts your request traces and replays them preserving inter-arrival and size distributions
- can inject network latency when needed
- supports cold-start, warm-start, and sustained load modes
- captures TTFT, TPOT, queueing time, kernel exec time, and serialization time per request
- outputs histograms, raw samples, and per-window quantiles

[06:34] Priya: when you say replay preserves inter-arrival, does that include bursting behavior?
[06:38] Leah: yes we can replay bursts from traces or create synthetic ramps to reach 2x/3x. we'll also support user-defined ramp profiles.
[06:46] Jamal: and for metrics ingestion, can we stream metrics into our prometheus stack?
[06:50] Carlos: we can export metrics via prometheus remote write or pushgateway, or we can push CSVs; for the POC we usually share both the raw CSV and add a prometheus endpoint if you want real-time dashboards.
[07:02] Evan: regarding KV cache — is the priming step something you do automatically? we worry that first-run numbers will look terrible because of cold kv cache.
[07:10] Leah: we'll include a priming phase in the harness. we'll report both cold-run numbers and warm-run numbers with the cache primed. We also capture cache hit rates so you can see how much prefix reuse helps.
[07:21] Priya: please make sure the report separates queuing effects from pure inference; sometimes our orchestration is the bottleneck not the model.
[07:27] Carlos: agreed — we'll separate queueing and service times. we'll also log concurrency and GPU utilization.
[07:33] Jamal: are there recommended p95/p99 thresholds you see for typical payment workloads?
[07:38] Leah: broadly for interactive financial UIs, teams aim for TTFT p95 < 200 ms. For high-frequency backend rerankers, TPOT p95 under 500-700 ms is common on optimized 7B quantized models. But your current numbers (p95 210ms) are already close; we should be able to meet or improve on that.
[07:56] Priya: what about measurement noise and sampling? how many requests do we need to have stable p99 estimates?
[08:02] Leah: p99 can be noisy; best practice is to collect at least tens of thousands of samples per window. over the 10–15 minute windows at 120 rps you'll get plenty of samples; for rare bursts you may need longer runs. We'll provide confidence intervals and note statistical uncertainty.
[08:19] Carlos: let's capture per-minute sample counts in the report to show the reliability of quantiles.
[08:24] Jamal: okay. any security/compliance items in scope for this POC? we might need SOC2 docs before sharing production traces.
[08:33] Carlos: yes we can provide SOC2 attestation and standard security docs. if you need more, we can run the POC within a Dedicated VPC with customer-managed keys. we'll include the options in the scope doc.
[08:46] Priya: could you also include recommended auto-scaling rules? we want to avoid overprovisioning during spikes.
[08:51] Leah: we'll include autoscaling policy suggestions (target utilization, cooldowns) tied to the observed latency curves so you can balance cost vs latency.
[08:59] Marta: from product perspective we'd like a short summary we can share with directors — an executive one-pager with clear pass/fail.
[09:06] Carlos: we'll include an executive summary with clear pass/fail criteria and graphs for TTFT/TPOT at p95/p99.
[09:12] Jamal: great. final question: how do you handle model fallbacks and graceful degradation in Redwood? we want to avoid 5xx if capacity is saturated.
[09:21] Leah: Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to smaller model variants or to a degraded mode. we can simulate fallback during the stress test. the report will show how fallbacks affect latency and quality.
[09:32] Priya: sounds good. can you summarize the deliverables and timeline?
[09:36] Carlos: yes deliverables: POC scope doc + pricing (by 2025-01-30), benchmark harness and instructions (by 2025-02-05), one-week benchmark runs (target 2025-02-10 to 2025-02-17), final report with histograms, pass/fail and recommendations (by 2025-02-21).
[09:58] Jamal: we can align those dates. we'll aim to get traces within 72 hours.
[10:02] Carlos: perfect. any other outstanding risks?
[10:05] Evan: network peering setup time could delay start by a few days; we may run an initial benchmark with simulated latency to avoid stalls.
[10:12] Carlos: noted — we'll plan contingencies.
[10:15] Carlos: okay thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the scope doc and a calendar invite for the benchmarking window.
[10:20] Priya: thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
